title: Population 2005 (100 m, Mollweide)
description:
Modelled residential population per 100 m grid cell for 2005, from the JRC Global Human Settlement Layer GHS-POP R2023A. Values are persons per pixel on the World Mollweide grid (ESRI:54009), an equal-area projection, so a cell covers the same ground area everywhere and per-cell density needs no latitude correction. Coverage is 332 tiles of 10000x10000 pixels. Ocean-only cells of the grid are not published upstream, and a further 43 tiles that upstream ships containing nothing but nodata are omitted here, since they carry no data and cannot hold the band statistics a renderer needs.

**This is a derived, lossy product; its pixels are not bit-identical to the source.** The source was converted to allow partial reads over HTTP, which the upstream ZIP packaging prevents. The data type was narrowed from Float64 to Float32, which is lossless here because the source values carry only single-precision information (verified: identical GDAL checksums). Compression is LERC_ZSTD with a per-pixel error bound of 0.01 persons per cell, which is lossy. Across a 68-tile sample, the published population differs from the source by -0.000559% (-5,592 people). The largest absolute change to a tile total was 1,605 people. Among tiles holding over a million people, the largest relative shift was 0.0139%. Relative percentages are largest on nearly empty tiles because the quantization step is fixed; the absolute error there is a fraction of one person. Internal overviews and embedded statistics were added; neither exists upstream. For measurements, see [why this mirror exists](https://github.com/nlebovits/ghsl/blob/main/docs/upstream-gaps.md).

Query recipes are in the [collection agent guide](AGENTS.md). The authoritative original remains [JRC's own distribution](https://human-settlement.emergency.copernicus.eu/download.php?ds=pop).

thumbnail.title: Population 2005, global preview
thumbnail.description: Rendered from this collection's own COGs, downsampled through their internal overviews. Colour breaks follow the distribution of populated cells. Ocean is transparent and land with no residents is grey, so the two read differently.
